source.title: On the Edge of Memorization in Diffusion Models
source.authors: Sam Buchanan; Druv Pai; Yi-Ting Ma; Valentin De Bortoli

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures held-out test loss across model sizes in diffusion-denoiser settings and specifically argues that classical double descent does not apply straightforwardly to diffusion models. Its tested model class and measurements differ from the original deep-network double-descent studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out test-loss curves over model size in Figures 2 and 5, with qualitative discussion of generalization ending as memorization begins. It also reports memorization-ratio curves over model size. Training-loss comparisons and cited double-descent results are not rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: The study is about memorization in diffusion models. Its held-out test-loss sweeps over denoiser size M run only from N/10 up to M=N, which is the point where the model can fully memorize. No model past that point is trained, so its results cannot show whether risk falls again beyond interpolation, the part V4 asserts. The only bearing on double descent is a conceptual argument in Appendix G. It says the unique training-loss minimizer in diffusion is the memorizing denoiser, so double descent and benign overfitting 'do not apply straightforwardly'. No measured result past the threshold backs this argument, so it is discussion, not a test. No verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a training-loss crossover between a partially memorizing denoiser and the generalizing denoiser predicts the model size where memorization dominates, fitted as about (4/5)N with very low error. The remark that double descent and benign overfitting do not straightforwardly apply is a side argument in Appendix G, not a main conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates parameterized Gaussian-mixture diffusion denoisers and tracks held-out loss and memorization; it does not use the original double-descent model classes or interpolation-risk analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The experiments cover isotropic and low-rank Gaussian-mixture data settings; the memorization threshold is predicted using a fitted loss weighting.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix G argues that in diffusion the unique training-loss minimizer is the memorizing denoiser. Past a point, adding parameters never lowers training loss, so double descent and benign overfitting do not straightforwardly apply. The supporting nesting result is in Appendix B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For diffusion denoisers, capacity beyond the memorization point cannot yield a second descent, because the memorizing denoiser is the unique training-loss optimum.

fits_no_version.finding: As M grows, test loss stays near that of the ground-truth denoiser, then rises sharply at the generalization-to-memorization transition, predicted at about (4/5)N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Gaussian-mixture diffusion denoisers, held-out loss deteriorates only when memorization begins, at a capacity predicted by a training-loss crossover.

record.problems: The held-out test-loss trends relevant to V4 are shown in figures without numerical values or a textual account of the post-transition curve. The main model-size experiments use synthetic Gaussian-mixture settings; the low-rank image setting is also synthetic.
record.rows_left_out: Training-loss curves and comparisons with the ground-truth and memorizing surrogate denoisers were left out because they do not measure held-out risk. Appendix H.5 learned-variance and mean-distance measurements were also left out because they are not test-error measures for the listed versions.

untested.parts: Deep-network model-wise test error; no deep networks are trained.
Test error over training epochs is not reported.
Test error as N increases near the threshold is not reported. The N sweep is used only to fit the transition location.
Behaviour of risk past the interpolation point (M>N) is not measured.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs and samples.
Label noise, multiple peaks and tuned regularization are not tested.
Complexity is not recounted with an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Conceptual argument that double descent does not apply straightforwardly to diffusion models
Seed-robustness rerun of the Figure 2 test-loss and memorization curves (three seeds, very small error bars)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' with a V4 limits_scope label is downgraded. The test-loss figures stop at M=N, so they cannot bear on post-interpolation recovery, and the double-descent statement is an untested argument. The model class is M-component Gaussian-mixture denoisers on synthetic data.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test deep-network test error over model size or the fall-rise-fall shape near an interpolation threshold.
Training lasts 50,000 epochs in Section 4.1 and 100,000 epochs in Section 4.2, but the study does not report test error over epochs.
The study varies sample count in a sweep to predict the memorization transition, but does not report test error as sample count increases near that transition.
The study tests model-size trends in Gaussian-mixture diffusion denoisers, not a broad range of model classes; the full risk curve's behavior past the transition is not described in text.
The study predicts a model-size memorization transition from a training-loss crossover, but does not test one effective-complexity measure across model size, epochs, and sample count.
The study does not test label-noise causes, multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a peak.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether this changes a double-descent curve into a U-shaped curve.
